1:
Keil and Delitzsch place the vision in its sequence: after the prophet had seen the glory of the Lord enter the new temple and had received the law to be announced concerning the service Israel was to render there, a stream of living water was shown him, proceeding from the threshold, flowing to the plain and emptying into the Dead Sea, to fertilise the barren soil and fill its salt water with vital power; and then the command about the boundaries of the land, its division among the tribes, and the building of the city.

Whether these are real waters is settled early and firmly. Henry argues from the necessity of a spiritual meaning here to a spiritual meaning in the rest of the vision: it cannot be the water brought by pipes for washing the sacrifices and keeping the temple clean and carried off again, for that would turn this pleasant river into a common sewer. Clarke puts it more bluntly still: literally no such waters were ever in the temple, and because there were none Solomon had the brazen sea made; the water for it might have been brought in pipes, but a fountain yielding abundance was not there and could not be there on the top of such a hill. Wesley alone reads it as plumbing, the fountain lying to the west and the conduit pipes laid to bring water to the temple, one main pipe perhaps running under the east gate. Henry takes the waters for the gospel going out from Jerusalem and spreading into the countries about, and observes that the prophet had walked round the house again and again without noticing them until now, since God makes his mind known to his people not all at once but by degrees.

On the course of the stream Ellicott is precise. The door is the entrance of the temple itself, and though the waters issue from the threshold at the centre of the east front and their general course is due east, they had to be deflected a little southward at the start in order to pass the porch and the altar and both gateways. Gill places the prophet brought back from the outer court to the door leading into the holiest. Clarke traces the route further, past the altar of burnt offering on the right and so eastward to fall into the brook and thence to the Dead Sea. Ellicott explains why the prophet was taken out by the north gate, the east gate being shut.

The measuring is the heart of the passage. Ellicott does the arithmetic: the whole distance is four thousand cubits, less than a mile and a half, during which the waters swell without any external addition from a streamlet to an impassable river, in direct opposition to the ordinary course of nature; a large part of that distance lay within the precincts already described, but the prophet takes no notice of it, since the whole is ideal and the precincts set forth one truth while the river sets forth another. The point, he says, is the increase of the kingdom of God, the same truth illustrated in the parable of the mustard seed. Clarke reports that the waters at first only oozed or dropped out, and applies the four stages three ways: to the gradual discovery of the plan of salvation, to the growth of a believer from seed to blade to ear to full corn, and to the successive discoveries a penitent receives, the grace of God appearing to come drop by drop and given as it can be used, a seed of light that multiplies itself. Gill takes the four measurings for four remarkable seasons of gospel preaching, and reads the man with the line as measuring by the rule of scripture, which is straight, whereas error has its windings and turnings.
6:
Ellicott corrects a small thing in the English: the prophet does not return to the brink, for he had never left it, but is told to pass along it, the word rendered brink here and bank in the next verse being the same. Gill takes the question put to him as an invitation to observe the rise and progress of the stream, how from small beginnings it became within two or three miles a deep and impassable river. On the course, Ellicott identifies the country as the Jordan valley and prefers the marginal plain to desert, meaning the widening of that valley north of the Dead Sea; the river has run due east so far, and now, without any mention of the Jordan, apparently takes its place and flows into the sea.

The healing of the sea draws the strongest language. Wesley says the waters shall be made wholesome, and that where the grace of God flows from the temple and altar it heals the corrupt nature of man and turns terrible deserts into a land of waters and gardens. Ellicott explains the healing as a change from being incapable of supporting life to being the home of life in all abundance and variety. He also handles a textual oddity: the pointing gives the two rivers, which has caused perplexity, especially since another prophet divides the waters between two seas; but only one river is meant here, and the dual form may allude to the Jordan flowing with it, or more likely express greatness, a double river, or by a division of the word become river of the sea. Clarke reads the fish as genuine converts and the fishers as the apostles, who were fishers of men.

The two fountains named give Ellicott another problem. The first is a well known copious spring about midway on the western coast of the Dead Sea; the second occurs only here and has not been certainly identified, one ancient writer placing it where the Jordan joins the sea, while others take the dual form of the name to mark one of the double cities of Moab and so place it on the eastern side, which Ellicott thinks more probable, since the phrase would then mean the whole breadth of the sea. Clarke places both at the southern and northern ends and takes the variety of the fish for all the nations and kindreds called by a gospel that is not exclusive like the system it replaced.

The unhealed marshes are the exception that completes the picture. Ellicott describes the ground: the southern end of the sea is very shallow and beyond it lies an extensive tract of very low land, overflowed when the river floods and left bare and encrusted with salt as it subsides. This shows, he says, that the prophet did not imagine the river running on through the valley to the southern sea, and that the effect of the life-giving waters ceases where the waters themselves cease to flow; and in the thing signified it shows we are not to expect a perfect and universal obedience as the effect of the gospel, since man is left free to hear or forbear. Gill takes the miry places for ditches and lakes lying near the sea but separate from it. On the trees Ellicott answers an objection to the spiritual reading, that nothing can be made of the fishermen: in every figure there must be details necessary to the figure which have nothing answering to them in the thing signified, and this prophet habitually carries such details very far; on a literal reading the fishermen would have no place at all, since there would be no such men in a glorified land. Clarke reads the unfailing fruit and the leaf for medicine of the fruits of the Spirit and the profession of the righteous.
13:
Gill argues from the measurements themselves. The border described here is different from and much larger than the land in the time of Moses or Joshua, and larger than it was either before or after the captivity; so the passage must be understood either of Canaan as it will be when the Jews are converted and possess it, or rather of the church, which is far greater than it was under the former dispensation and will be more extensive still when the kingdom reaches from sea to sea.

Henry moves from the sanctuary to the state. The land is secured to them by an oath: God lifted up his hand to give it to their fathers, and though the possession had been long discontinued he had not forgotten what he swore. Providences may for a time seem to contradict the promise, Henry says, but the promise will take place at last, and the heavenly Canaan is sure to all the seed on the same ground, being promised by one who cannot lie. He notes that the boundaries are fixed both ways, so that they must not encroach on their neighbours nor their neighbours on them, and that where the earlier survey began and ended at the salt sea this one begins and ends in the north; it is God who appoints the bounds of our habitation.

Ellicott observes what the division assumes: in the ideal land of the restoration not two tribes only but all twelve are to have portions, and since Levi is otherwise provided for in the oblation, Joseph takes two portions, as the earlier history required. The Hebrew says simply Joseph portions in the plural, he notes, since that they should be two and no more was a matter of course not needing to be specified. Clarke and Wesley both name the two sons who received them. Gill reads the equal inheritance spiritually, that true Israelites share alike in the same church state and its privileges, being all one.

Ellicott then does something none of the others attempt. The equality, he says, is generally and rightly understood of the width of the strips assigned to each tribe, since the vision throughout makes little account of the natural features of the country; but he notices in passing that this makes the actual areas very unequal, the country being nearly three times as broad at the south as at the north, so that the southern tribes would have nearly three times as much land while being ideally equal. Were the portions made actually equal, he adds, the map would be much changed: the oblation would move considerably south with ample room between the two seas, its northern line falling a little north of Jerusalem and its southern within ten or twelve miles of Beersheba, and the temple standing a few miles north-west of Hebron, still on the western watershed.
15:
Ellicott sets this survey beside the older one. The boundaries are essentially those given to Moses, only that there the southern is described first, for a people coming up from Egypt, while here the northern comes first, for a people supposed to be returning from Babylon; the older account has more detail, and since the points named are the same it is fair to fill this one out from it. What he finds remarkable is that in both the eastern boundary is the Jordan: the inheritance of the tribes east of the river was a modification of the original allotment and is not taken into account here at all, so that portions are assigned on the west of the river to the two and a half tribes who had lived east of it through the whole history. At the eastern border he notes that the word rendered from means literally from between, the line running between the territories of Hauran and Damascus and Gilead on one side and Israel on the other.

The identifications are mostly uncertain and Ellicott says so. The line begins at the Mediterranean, but at what point cannot be determined, since although the tribal lines were straight and parallel it does not appear whether they ran perpendicular to the Jordan or to the sea. Hethlon is mentioned only here and once after, has not been identified, and was probably of little importance, since it is located only by reference to another place. Hamath is not the city on the Orontes, much too far north, but the district; the defile leading to it is many miles long and authorities differ over which end should be called its entrance. Berothah lay between Hamath and Damascus but nothing more is known of it; Sibraim may be a place named in the older list and stood on the confines of two kingdoms; of the middle Hazar all that is known is that it lay on the border of Hauran, used here more widely than the classical name. Clarke offers his own equivalents for several of these and remarks candidly of some that these things are very uncertain. Gill notices that the description begins on the north side, and reads even that as significant.

Ellicott also gives the dimensions. At the northern boundary the whole width of the country would be somewhat over thirty miles. The eastern line runs beyond the mouth of the Jordan to the southern end of the Dead Sea and thence to the waters of strife, so that the extreme length of the land, though uncertain, must have fallen short of two hundred and fifty miles. From there the boundary strikes across the mountainous desert to the river of Egypt and follows it to the sea, the southern line measuring nearly a hundred miles along the curve or about eighty-seven from east to west. Keil and Delitzsch work at the same southern boundary and report a conjecture identifying one of its points with a place that held a Roman garrison. Clarke and Wesley both identify that river and the sea at its mouth.

The strangers close the chapter and every voice takes the same view. Clarke states the novelty plainly: in the former divisions no place was given to strangers, but in this one, which he says can have no reference but to the gospel since no such division ever literally took place, the strangers are to have an inheritance, which intimates the calling of the Gentiles. Wesley says it certainly looks at gospel times, when the partition wall between Jew and Gentile was taken down and both put on a level. Gill reads it of any congregation nearest which such sojourners settle and to which they offer themselves, where they shall be readily admitted; and Wesley notes that their children were to be invested with the right of inheriting from their birth.
